The github-actions update group in dependabot.yml has no `cooldown` setting, so a newly published action version can be proposed the same day it is released, before the community has had a chance to flag a compromised release. This is a real, minor supply-chain hardening gap in the project's own update configuration (not a test fixture): adding a short cooldown (e.g. a few days) would reduce exposure to a freshly-compromised action version. Any update it proposes still goes through CI and review before merging, which limits the practical impact.

verdicts.what: .github/workflows/api-docs.yml:27, credential persistence through GitHub Actions artifacts: does not set persist-credentials: false
verdicts.reason: Flags `actions/checkout` without `persist-credentials: false`. Outside test.yml and lint.yml (judged separately), every workflow this fires in (api-docs, containers, crewai-macos, cross-os, full-gate, images, images-refresh, release, samples, wiki) triggers only on `push` to specific branches/tags/paths, `workflow_dispatch`, `workflow_call` or `schedule` -- never on `pull_request` -- so no externally-supplied code ever runs in the job while the persisted token is on disk; all of it is maintainer- or schedule-triggered.

verdicts.what: .github/workflows/api-docs.yml:43, Github Action from Unverified Creator used
verdicts.reason: Flags third-party marketplace actions (gVisor/uv/etc. setup actions) not carrying GitHub's "verified creator" badge, across api-docs, containers, crewai-macos, cross-os, images, integration, lint, release, samples and test. A fork's `pull_request` run (the only externally-triggerable case, in test.yml/lint.yml) gets GitHub's automatically read-only, secret-less token regardless of which actions a workflow calls, and every other workflow this fires in is maintainer-dispatched or schedule-only: nothing here gives an outside contributor a way to turn a compromised action into access it does not already have.

Outside test.yml and lint.yml (judged separately), every workflow this fires in (api-docs, containers, crewai-macos, cross-os, full-gate, images, images-refresh, release, samples, wiki) triggers only on `push` to specific branches/tags/paths, `workflow_dispatch`, `workflow_call` or `schedule` -- never on `pull_request` -- so no externally-supplied code ever runs in the job while the persisted token is on disk; all of it is maintainer- or schedule-triggered.

verdicts.what: .github/workflows/samples.yml:86, Github Action from Unverified Creator used
verdicts.reason: Flags third-party marketplace actions (gVisor/uv/etc. setup actions) not carrying GitHub's "verified creator" badge, across api-docs, containers, crewai-macos, cross-os, images, integration, lint, release, samples and test. A fork's `pull_request` run (the only externally-triggerable case, in test.yml/lint.yml) gets GitHub's automatically read-only, secret-less token regardless of which actions a workflow calls, and every other workflow this fires in is maintainer-dispatched or schedule-only: nothing here gives an outside contributor a way to turn a compromised action into access it does not already have.

test.yml has no top-level `permissions:` block and triggers on `pull_request` for any branch (including forks). Nothing in its jobs currently writes with the token, so I found no concrete abuse path, but an unscoped ambient token in a fork-reachable, no-approval-gate workflow is worth minimizing explicitly (e.g. `permissions: contents: read`) rather than relying on org defaults.

verdicts.what: .github/workflows/test.yml:24, credential persistence through GitHub Actions artifacts: does not set persist-credentials: false
verdicts.reason: test.yml triggers on `pull_request` for any branch, which includes forked contributions, and checks out the PR's own code (then runs the unit/lint/provider-smoke suites against it) without `persist-credentials: false`. A step that runs PR-supplied code in the same job as the persisted credential is the classic artipacked pattern. GitHub automatically restricts the ambient `GITHUB_TOKEN` for a fork `pull_request` to read-only with no secrets, which caps the real impact, but that is GitHub's default behaviour, not something this workflow configures -- add `persist-credentials: false` to remove the gap outright.

verdicts.reason: No HEALTHCHECK instruction in the shipped python-sb base image. An operational/availability nicety, not an attacker-reachable gap; kept open since it is a real, if minor, gap in a file that builds what ships.

verdicts.what: Dockerfile:1, Ensure that a user for the container has been created
verdicts.reason: checkov's own version of the missing-USER finding above: no user is created for this shipped base image.

verdicts.what: Dockerfile:1, Image user should not be 'root'
verdicts.reason: This is the `python-sb` base image `make build-image-base` ships (FROM python:3.11-slim, no USER set, so it runs as root), and every other provider Dockerfile (Dockerfile-landlock, Dockerfile-unshare, etc.) builds FROM it without adding one either. Its own header comment says it has "No OS provider (no unshare, bwrap, firejail, qemu)" baked in, so nothing here needs root privileges the way unshare-based providers do: adding a non-root USER would cost nothing and is a real, if modest, defense-in-depth gap -- if the Python-level guards were ever bypassed, the escaping process would have root inside the container.
Same image and same root-user gap as DS-0002 on this file; trivy's second rule on the same missing-USER condition.

Checked guard_files.py:445 (`_TMP_FALLBACK = "/tmp"`, a comment-documented mirror of tempfile.gettempdir()'s own fallback), client_subprocess_sse_daemon.py:865 (`tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="pysb_", dir="/tmp")`, a securely random unique directory, not a predictable shared path), and the *_sse_daemon.py/qemu_setup.py/smolvm_sse_daemon.py hits (`/tmp/run_pysandbox_bootstrap.sh`, `/tmp/pysb.sock`, the gvisor bundle's `/tmp` tmpfs mount): these are paths inside the sandboxed guest's own isolated filesystem/namespace, never a host path other local users could race. docker_sandbox_daemon.py's `_PASSWD_HOME = "/tmp"` names a container-internal convention, not a host temp file. No instance writes attacker-influenced content to a predictable host-shared path.

pysandboxes/remote/config_stream.py's `load_config_from_fd` and main_sandbox.py:417 both unpickle configuration read from a named pipe or fd that only the trusted parent process (the host pysandboxes process that spawned this child) ever writes to -- both sites carry an explicit comment to that effect ("Payload written by the trusted parent", "noqa: S301 - written by the trusted parent"). The untrusted, sandboxed program is the child here, and it cannot write to its own parent's named pipe before the parent does; no attacker-controlled bytes reach `pickle.loads`.

All six hits are best-effort cleanup in daemon teardown, each with an inline comment explaining why swallowing the exception is safe: bwrap_sse_daemon.py:771 (killing an already-gone slirp4netns process), slirp4netns_common.py:124 ("it fails closed: a forward that slirp4netns refused simply does not exist"), unshare_sse_daemon.py:444/590/615/761 (unlinking a config FIFO the child already consumed, or other teardown steps where the failure mode is a stale temp entry, never an unguarded sandbox). None of these swallow a check that would otherwise block an attacker.

guard_socket.py's two hits are the guard's own wildcard-address detection (`_resolve_wildcard_host` turns `bind(("", port))` into the literal `"0.0.0.0"` the network rules are written against) -- it is analysis code, not a listening socket. The pysandboxes/remote/*_sse_daemon.py hits bind the host<->sandboxed-child IPC control server inside the private network namespace unshare/bwrap/gvisor/qemu already create for that sandbox, so binding every interface there reaches only that isolated namespace, never the host's real network. samples/mcp-server-demo's bind is the demo's own local server, run by whoever starts the sample.
